name: Mona Lisa
kicker: Leonardo da Vinci’s portrait in the Louvre · The world’s most famous smile
briefing: She has been smiling for more than 500 years, and people still cannot agree on why. Around 1503, Leonardo da Vinci began this small portrait using sfumato, a soft, smoky blending technique with no harsh outlines, and may have kept reworking it for over a decade. Stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and parodied by artists ever since, she is now the most famous painting on Earth.

sample.note: 8 real QBReader tossups (4 Middle School/Easy High School + 4 Regular High School, power-marked); one Regular HS tossup’s actual answer was “Theft of the Mona Lisa,” the 1911 heist, not the painting

tossups.p: This woman is traditionally identified as Lisa del Giocondo, wife of a Florentine silk merchant, and a 2005 discovery of a margin note helped confirm that identification. A hazy, invented landscape of icy mountains and a winding road fills the space behind her.
tossups.r: Infrared scans suggest her once-visible eyebrows faded over the centuries. For 10 points, name this small portrait by Leonardo da Vinci, famous for its subject’s enigmatic smile.

tossups.p: Marcel Duchamp added a mustache and goatee to a postcard of this work in his 1919 piece _L.H.O.O.Q._ Andy Warhol later silkscreened thirty repeated copies of it in a 1963 work called _Thirty Are Better Than One_.
tossups.r: Its subject’s hands are folded on the arm of her chair. For 10 points, name this portrait of a woman with an enigmatic smile, painted by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: In 1911, a Louvre employee named Vincenzo Peruggia hid this painting under his coat and walked out of the museum, keeping it in his apartment for over two years. Police questioned the poet Guillaume Apollinaire and his friend Pablo Picasso before both were cleared.
tossups.r: Leonardo da Vinci painted its subject using his soft, smoky sfumato technique. For 10 points, name this painting of a woman with an enigmatic smile, stolen from the Louvre.

tossups.p: A second, earlier-looking version of this painting, nicknamed the “Isleworth” version, may have been partly painted by the same artist. The traditional identification of its sitter as Lisa del Giocondo comes mainly from the 16th-century biographer Giorgio Vasari [“vah-ZAH-ree”].
tossups.r: The sitter in this painting has no visible eyebrows or eyelashes. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci portrait of a woman with a mysterious smile, housed in the Louvre.

tossups.p: Salvador Dalí once posed as the subject of this painting in a photographic self-portrait that puts his own famous mustache onto her face. Its subject is traditionally said to be the wife of silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo.
tossups.r: A winding road and a distant bridge appear in the hazy landscape behind her. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci painting famous for its enigmatic smile.

tossups.p: This painting is likely nicknamed in Italian and French after its sitter’s married surname, Giocondo. Leonardo da Vinci probably began this oil-on-poplar-panel work around 1503 and may have kept reworking it for over a decade afterward.
tossups.r: The sitter’s hands rest folded on the arm of her chair. For 10 points, name this portrait of a woman with a famously enigmatic smile, now displayed in the Louvre.

tossups.p: Pop artist Jasper Johns referenced this painting, alongside a white handprint, in his work _Figure 7_. Decades earlier, Marcel Duchamp had drawn a mustache and goatee on a cheap postcard reproduction of it.
tossups.r: Leonardo da Vinci used his soft sfumato blending technique throughout this portrait. For 10 points, name this famously smiling painting stolen from the Louvre in 1911.

tossups.p: After this painting vanished in 1911, a Louvre employee named Vincenzo Peruggia eventually tried to sell it to a dealer in Florence, which led to his arrest. Before he was caught, French police had briefly suspected and questioned the artist Pablo Picasso.
tossups.r: This oil-on-wood portrait shows no visible eyebrows on its subject. For 10 points, name this painting by Leonardo da Vinci, famous for an enigmatic smile.

tossups.p: Infrared analysis in 2007 suggested that this painting’s subject may once have had visible eyebrows and eyelashes that faded over time. A margin note discovered in 2005, written by an assistant to a Florentine official, helped confirm the sitter’s identity as Lisa del Giocondo.
tossups.r: Andy Warhol silkscreened thirty copies of this painting in 1963. For 10 points, name this small Leonardo da Vinci portrait known for its mysterious half-smile.

tossups.p: Behind this painting’s subject, a hazy landscape recedes into icy mountains and a winding path leading to a distant bridge. Giorgio Vasari’s 1550 biography of the artist identified the sitter as the wife of Francesco del Giocondo.
tossups.r: This portrait was painted in oil on a poplar wood panel, not canvas. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci painting of a woman with an enigmatic smile.

tossups.p: This painting’s Italian and French nicknames both derive from her husband’s surname, Giocondo. Leonardo da Vinci likely began painting her around 1503 and may have continued reworking the piece for over a decade.
tossups.r: A 1911 theft of this painting from the Louvre kept it missing for over two years. For 10 points, name this famously smiling portrait, stolen by Vincenzo Peruggia.

tossups.p: This painting’s wood panel is made of poplar, and its paint includes Leonardo da Vinci’s characteristic sfumato blending in the folds of the sitter’s dark hair and veil. A separate, earlier-looking “Isleworth” version may have also come partly from Leonardo’s own hand.
tossups.r: The woman in this portrait is traditionally identified as Lisa del Giocondo. For 10 points, name this small painting in the Louvre, famous for an enigmatic smile.

tossups.p: Guillaume Apollinaire and Pablo Picasso were both briefly questioned by police after this painting disappeared from the Louvre in 1911. The thief, museum employee Vincenzo Peruggia, hid it in his apartment before trying to sell it in Florence.
tossups.r: This small portrait shows its subject with no visible eyebrows. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci painting known for an enigmatic smile.

tossups.p: Marcel Duchamp’s 1919 work _L.H.O.O.Q._ added a mustache and goatee to a cheap postcard copy of this painting. Andy Warhol paid tribute to it after its 1963 visit to the United States with a multi-panel silkscreen called _Thirty Are Better Than One_.
tossups.r: Its sitter is traditionally identified as the wife of merchant Francesco del Giocondo. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci portrait famous for its subject’s mysterious smile.

tossups.p: This painting’s subject rests her folded hands on the arm of a wooden chair, in front of a hazy, invented landscape with a winding road and a distant bridge. The sitter is traditionally identified, based on Giorgio Vasari’s writings, as Lisa del Giocondo.
tossups.r: Leonardo da Vinci used his soft sfumato technique throughout this small portrait. For 10 points, name this painting famous for an enigmatic smile, on display in the Louvre.

trap.title: The Painting, or the Heist?
trap.body: Some real tossups ask about the famous 1911 theft itself as its own separate answer — “Theft of the Mona Lisa” — packed with clues about Vincenzo Peruggia, Guillaume Apollinaire, and Pablo Picasso being questioned by police. Buzzing “Mona Lisa” on one of those is a wrong, early guess.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This woman,” “this painting,” or “this portrait” means the painting itself. “This crime,” “this theft,” or “this event” means the 1911 heist — a related but separate answer line.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mona Lisa (or La Gioconda/La Joconde); a separate answer line, the Theft of the Mona Lisa, covers the 1911 heist itself.
